analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off the New England coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and a subcommittee from January 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit the Interior Department from leasing any area of the outer Continental Shelf off the coasts of Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Connecticut for oil or gas exploration, development, or production [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Rep. David Cicilline with 20 New England Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S4]. It never advanced past a subcommittee referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities and businesses in the five New England states: commercial fishermen whose grounds would be shielded from an oil spill, tourism and recreation businesses along the shore, and towns whose economies depend on a clean coastline. Permanent protection matters because a single Interior Department plan could otherwise open these waters to leasing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: New England coastal towns, fishermen, and tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 8 of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Interior Secretary may not issue any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas in any area of the outer Continental Shelf off Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, or Connecticut [S3].

The protection is written into permanent law, 'notwithstanding any other provision' of the leasing statute, so it cannot be undone by a future administration's leasing plan without a new act of Congress [S3].
It covers all five New England coastal states, closing the region off as a block rather than leaving each lease decision to the Interior Department's periodic five-year plans [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which would lose any chance to bid on New England offshore leases, and federal and state treasuries, which forgo any royalties such leasing might have produced. Consumers see no meaningful cost: New England offshore waters are not a significant current source of oil or gas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking offshore access

drawbacks.text: The ban forecloses any future domestic energy production and the federal and state royalty revenue that offshore leasing can generate, even if drilling technology later made some extraction far safer than it is today [S2][S3].
A permanent statutory ban removes flexibility: if the nation ever faced an oil supply emergency, Congress would have to pass new legislation before any of these waters could be considered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to New England is concrete and one-sided: a spill off these coasts would hit fisheries, tourism, and shoreline towns hard, and the region is not a meaningful oil or gas producer today. The cost is foregone potential revenue and energy supply, which is real but speculative. On the whole, a well-designed protection whose main cost falls on an industry that currently gets nothing from these waters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2019, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the Congress and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, with 20 New England Democratic cosponsors listed at introduction [S1][S3][S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and on February 5, 2019, referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, never left committee, and received no action after the subcommittee referral for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: New England offshore waters remained legally open to future oil and gas leasing, so the oil and gas industry kept its potential access while coastal communities kept living with the risk a leasing plan could have brought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies kept potential offshore access

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently bar oil and gas leasing off the New England coast.

for.name: 20 of 231 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, all from the five New England states

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; no markup ever scheduled
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without a hearing, markup, or vote for two years; it was sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee in February 2019 and never advanced further.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: His administration's draft offshore leasing plan proposed opening new areas of the outer Continental Shelf to drilling, the policy backdrop against which New England members introduced permanent protections.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 original sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats from the five New England states, and the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors before dying in committee [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would end any possibility of leasing New England outer Continental Shelf waters for exploration, development, or production [S2][S3]. An oil spill in these waters would fall on fishing grounds and shorelines rather than on the companies drilling them, so the industry's interest runs against the coastal communities this bill protects.

Fishing grounds off Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut would be shielded from drilling activity and the spill risk that comes with it, the same outcome coastal economies want.
Beaches and shorelines in the five states would be protected from the visual and environmental impact of offshore drilling, which directly supports tourism-dependent towns.
